subChunks.title: Maps: HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap
subChunks.hookHtml: A List keeps things in sequence; a Set keeps things unique. But what if you need to look something up by name? That is the Map's domain — a key-value registry where each key unlocks its associated value in constant time.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Map Interface: Core Operations

All Map implementations share the same core API. put(key, value) stores an entry, get(key) retrieves it (returning null if absent), containsKey(key) checks existence, and remove(key) deletes an entry.

Map<String, Integer> spellDamage = new HashMap<>();
spellDamage.put("Fireball", 80);
spellDamage.put("Frost", 60);
spellDamage.put("Thunder", 90);

System.out.println(spellDamage.get("Fireball"));       // 80
System.out.println(spellDamage.get("Earthquake"));      // null
System.out.println(spellDamage.containsKey("Thunder")); // true
spellDamage.remove("Frost");
System.out.println(spellDamage.size());                 // 2

// Safe retrieval with default
int dmg = spellDamage.getOrDefault("Unknown", 0);
System.out.println(dmg); // 0

Iterating Over a Map

Use entrySet() to iterate all key-value pairs. keySet() gives only keys; values() gives only values.

Map<String, Integer> registry = new HashMap<>();
registry.put("Fireball", 80);
registry.put("Frost", 60);
registry.put("Thunder", 90);

// entrySet() — most common
for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> entry : registry.entrySet()) {
    System.out.println(entry.getKey() + ": " + entry.getValue());
}

// With streams
registry.entrySet().stream()
    .sorted(Map.Entry.comparingByKey())
    .forEach(e -> System.out.println(e.getKey() + " -> " + e.getValue()));

// Map.of() — immutable factory (Java 9+)
Map<String, Integer> fixed = Map.of("Arc", 20, "Zap", 15);

HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap

All three implement Map, but they differ in ordering guarantees:

// HashMap — unordered, fastest O(1) operations
Map<String,Integer> hash = new HashMap<>();
hash.put("C", 3); hash.put("A", 1); hash.put("B", 2);
// iteration order is unpredictable

// LinkedHashMap — insertion order preserved
Map<String,Integer> linked = new LinkedHashMap<>();
linked.put("C", 3); linked.put("A", 1); linked.put("B", 2);
linked.forEach((k,v) -> System.out.print(k + " ")); // C A B

// TreeMap — sorted by key (natural or Comparator)
Map<String,Integer> tree = new TreeMap<>();
tree.put("C", 3); tree.put("A", 1); tree.put("B", 2);
tree.forEach((k,v) -> System.out.print(k + " ")); // A B C

Useful Map Methods (Java 8+)

Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();

// putIfAbsent — only insert if key missing
counts.putIfAbsent("Fireball", 0);

// merge — insert or update with a function
counts.merge("Fireball", 1, Integer::sum); // add 1 to existing, or set to 1
counts.merge("Fireball", 1, Integer::sum); // now Fireball = 2

// compute — update with a BiFunction
counts.compute("Fireball", (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 10);

storyBeats.text: The Academy Registrar's office is legendary: any apprentice can walk in, name a spell, and instantly receive its power rating. Behind this magic lies the Map — the most versatile data structure in Java.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A Map is the spellbook's index: every key unlocks a value. Give me 'Fireball' and I give you its damage. Give me an unknown spell and I give you null — or a safe default if you use getOrDefault().

storyBeats.speaker: HashMap Core API
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: But not all Maps are equal. HashMap gives you speed with no ordering guarantees. LinkedHashMap remembers the order you inserted entries. TreeMap sorts by key automatically. Choose based on what you need to do with the Map after filling it.

storyBeats.speaker: Three Map Types
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: To iterate over all entries, use entrySet() — it gives you Map.Entry objects with getKey() and getValue(). For word-frequency counting or grouping, the merge() method is particularly powerful.
The apprentice fills the Registry with spells and their damage values, iterates every entry, and instantly retrieves any spell by name. The Registrar nods with approval.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a spell damage registry using HashMap:

  1. Create a HashMap<String, Integer> and add: Fireball→80, Frost→60, Thunder→90, Heal→0.
  2. Look up Thunder's damage and print it in the format "Thunder: 90".
  3. Iterate over all entries using entrySet() and print each in the format "name: damage".
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap in your own words. Describe a scenario where you would choose each one, and why iteration order matters.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Recreate the spell damage registry from scratch. Build the HashMap, look up Thunder, and iterate all entries — no starter code provided.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A Java interface representing a collection of key-value pairs where each key is unique; common implementations include HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap.
A hash-table-based Map implementation offering O(1) average-case performance for get and put, but with no guaranteed iteration order.
A HashMap that additionally maintains a doubly-linked list of entries in insertion order, making iteration predictable.
A NavigableMap implementation based on a red-black tree; all keys are kept in sorted (natural or comparator-defined) order, with O(log n) operations.
A Map method that returns a Set of Map.Entry objects, each providing getKey() and getValue(), enabling full iteration over key-value pairs.
A Map method that returns the value for a key if present, or a specified default value if the key is absent — avoids null checks.
A Map method that inserts a value if the key is absent, or applies a remapping BiFunction to merge an existing value with the new one.

questions.questionHtml: Which Map implementation guarantees that keys are iterated in sorted order?
questions.explanationHtml: TreeMap is backed by a red-black tree and keeps all keys sorted according to their natural ordering (or a Comparator provided at construction time). This gives O(log n) performance for operations but guarantees alphabetical/numeric key ordering during iteration. HashMap makes no ordering guarantees. LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, not sorted order. HashSet is not a Map at all.

TreeMap sorts keys by natural ordering, which for Strings is alphabetical (lexicographic). Alphabetically: Arc < Fireball < Zap, so the forEach iterates in that order. If this were a HashMap, the order would be unpredictable.

questions.questionHtml: This code throws a NullPointerException. What is wrong and how would you fix it?
questions.correctAnswer: damage.get("Earthquake") returns null because the key is absent. Auto-unboxing null to int throws NullPointerException. Fix: use damage.getOrDefault("Earthquake", 0) or check containsKey() first.
questions.explanationHtml: get() returns null for absent keys. Assigning null to a primitive int variable triggers auto-unboxing, which calls null.intValue() and throws NullPointerException. The safe alternatives are: (1) use getOrDefault("Earthquake", 0) to provide a fallback; (2) store in Integer val (boxed) and null-check; or (3) check containsKey() before calling get().

questions.questionHtml: You are building a spell audit log that must display entries in the exact order they were added. Which Map is most appropriate?
questions.explanationHtml: LinkedHashMap extends HashMap and additionally maintains a doubly-linked list that records insertion order. When you iterate (via forEach, entrySet(), etc.), entries appear in the order they were put into the map. HashMap has unpredictable iteration order. TreeMap sorts by key, not by insertion time. EnumMap is specialised for enum keys and iterates in enum declaration order.

subChunks.title: Queues, Stacks & the Deque Interface
subChunks.hookHtml: Not every problem calls for random access — sometimes order of operations is everything. Queues serve first-come-first-served. Stacks remember what came last and undo it first. These are the fundamental orderings of task management, expression evaluation, and undo systems.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Deque Interface: Stack and Queue in One

Deque (Double-Ended Queue) is the Swiss Army knife of sequential data structures. ArrayDeque is its most efficient implementation. Use it as a stack (LIFO) or a queue (FIFO) — or both at the same time.

// As a STACK (LIFO — Last In, First Out)
Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push("Fireball");  // adds to front
stack.push("Shield");
stack.push("Heal");
System.out.println(stack.pop());  // Heal  — most recently pushed
System.out.println(stack.pop());  // Shield
System.out.println(stack.pop());  // Fireball

// peek() — look without removing
stack.push("Arc");
System.out.println(stack.peek()); // Arc — still in stack

ArrayDeque as a Queue

For FIFO (First In, First Out) behaviour, use offer() to enqueue and poll() to dequeue. Prefer these over add()/remove() for queue use — they return null/false on failure rather than throwing exceptions.

// As a QUEUE (FIFO — First In, First Out)
Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
queue.offer("Fireball"); // enqueue at rear
queue.offer("Shield");
queue.offer("Heal");
System.out.println(queue.poll()); // Fireball — first in, first out
System.out.println(queue.poll()); // Shield
System.out.println(queue.peek()); // Heal — still in queue

PriorityQueue: Min-Heap Ordering

PriorityQueue<T> does not preserve insertion order. Instead, poll() always returns the smallest element according to natural ordering (or a custom Comparator). It implements Queue, not Deque.

PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
pq.offer(5);
pq.offer(1);
pq.offer(3);
pq.offer(2);
pq.offer(4);

while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
    System.out.print(pq.poll() + " "); // 1 2 3 4 5
}
// Always polls smallest first (min-heap)

// Max-heap — reverse the order:
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxPQ = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
maxPQ.offer(5); maxPQ.offer(1); maxPQ.offer(3);
while (!maxPQ.isEmpty()) {
    System.out.print(maxPQ.poll() + " "); // 5 3 1
}

Choosing the Right Structure

A quick decision guide:

// Need LIFO (undo, recursion simulation)?  -> ArrayDeque as stack
// Need FIFO (task queue, BFS)?             -> ArrayDeque as queue
// Need priority ordering (Dijkstra, jobs)? -> PriorityQueue
// Need iteration with access by index?     -> ArrayList

// Note: Stack class (legacy) and LinkedList work too,
// but ArrayDeque is preferred for stack/queue use cases.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's Spell Queue manages combat turns: the first spell cast fires first, the last one prepared fires last. The Order of Undoing uses a Stack — to reverse the most recent enchantment, you must pop the top of the casting history.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Lists are for storing things you'll access by position. Queues and stacks are for controlling the *order* of processing. These are not subtle distinctions — they change the entire character of your algorithm.

storyBeats.speaker: ArrayDeque as Stack
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The same ArrayDeque works as a queue when you use offer() and poll() instead of push() and pop(). offer() adds to the rear; poll() removes from the front — First In, First Out. Perfect for task scheduling.

storyBeats.speaker: PriorityQueue
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: PriorityQueue does not preserve insertion order. Internally it is a min-heap: poll() always gives you the smallest element. Reverse it with Comparator.reverseOrder() for a max-heap.
The apprentice implements both a spell history stack and a priority combat queue. Each data structure serves its purpose precisely — no more, no less.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Practice two data structures in one Main class:

  1. Use an ArrayDeque<String> as a stack. Push "Fireball", "Shield", and "Heal" (in that order). Then pop all three and print each — you should see LIFO order: Heal, Shield, Fireball.
  2. Use a PriorityQueue<Integer>. Add the values 5, 1, 3, 2, 4. Then poll all elements and print each — they should come out in ascending order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between a stack and a queue in your own words. Give a real-world example of each. Why does ArrayDeque work for both, and when would you use PriorityQueue instead?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Recreate both exercises from scratch — no starter code. Push three spells onto a stack and pop them in LIFO order; add five numbers to a PriorityQueue and poll them in ascending order.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A double-ended queue interface that supports adding and removing elements from both ends; can be used as either a stack or a queue.
A resizable array implementation of Deque that is faster than Stack and LinkedList for stack and queue operations, with no capacity restrictions.
Last In, First Out — the ordering principle of a stack; the most recently added element is the first to be removed (push/pop).
First In, First Out — the ordering principle of a queue; the first element added is the first to be removed (offer/poll).
A queue implementation backed by a min-heap; poll() always returns the smallest element according to natural ordering or a supplied Comparator.
A tree-based data structure where the parent node is always smaller than or equal to its children, allowing O(log n) insertion and O(1) minimum retrieval.
A Deque/Queue method that returns the head element without removing it; returns null if the queue is empty (unlike element() which throws).

questions.questionHtml: When using ArrayDeque as a stack, which method removes and returns the most recently added element?
questions.explanationHtml: pop() removes and returns the element at the front of the deque (the most recently pushed element in stack usage), giving LIFO behaviour. It throws NoSuchElementException if the deque is empty. peek() returns the front element without removing it. poll() and offer() are queue-style methods: offer() adds to the rear and poll() removes from the front — giving FIFO behaviour, not LIFO.

Comparator.reverseOrder() makes this a max-heap: poll() returns the largest element first. The elements are 3, 1, 4, 1. The largest is 4 — so first poll returns 4. The next largest is 3 — so second poll returns 3. Note that duplicate values (two 1s) are allowed in PriorityQueue.

questions.questionHtml: This code is meant to process elements in FIFO order but prints them in LIFO order. What is the bug?
questions.correctAnswer: push() and pop() implement stack (LIFO) behaviour. For FIFO, use offer() to add and poll() to remove. Replace push() with offer() and pop() with poll().
questions.explanationHtml: push() adds elements to the front of the deque, and pop() also removes from the front — giving LIFO (stack) order: Task C, Task B, Task A. For FIFO queue behaviour, use offer() (adds to rear) and poll() (removes from front), so elements are processed in the order they were added: Task A, Task B, Task C.

questions.questionHtml: You are implementing a spell suggestion feature: the most recently used spell should be suggested first (like browser history). Which data structure fits best?
options: TreeMap with spell names as keys
questions.explanationHtml: Browser history and 'most recently used' suggestions are classic stack (LIFO) use cases: the last item pushed is the first item returned. ArrayDeque as a stack (using push()/peek()/pop()) gives O(1) operations at both ends and is the most efficient choice. PriorityQueue orders by magnitude, not recency. TreeMap orders alphabetically. LinkedList as a queue gives FIFO — the opposite of what's needed.
